# Non-uniqueness of weak solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations in $R^3$

# Abstract

To our knowledge, the convex integration method has been widely applied to the study of non-uniqueness of solutions to the Naiver-Stokes equations in the periodic region, but there are few works on applying this method to the corresponding problems in the whole space or other regions. In this paper, we prove that weak solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations are not unique in the class of weak solutions with ﬁnite kinetic energy in the whole space, which extends the non uniqueness result for the Navier-Stokes equations on torus $\mathbb{T}^3$ in the groundbreaking work (Buckmaster and Vicol, Ann. of Math., 189 (2019), pp.101-144) to $\mathbb R^3$. The critical ingredients of the proof include developing an iterative scheme in which the approximation solution is refined by decomposing it into local and non-local parts. For the non-local part, we introduce the localized corrector which plays a crucial role in balancing the compact support of the Reynolds stress error with the non-compact support of the solution. As applications of this argument, we first prove that there exist infinitely many weak solutions that dissipate the kinetic energy in smooth bounded domain. Moreover, we show the instability of the Navier-Stokes equations near Couette flow in $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$.

*Keywords*: Navier-Stokes equations, Non-uniqueness, Convex integration method, Localization argument.

*Mathematics Subject Classification*: 35Q30, 76D03.

# 1 Introduction

In this paper, we consider the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in $\mathbb R^3$:

$$\left\{ \begin{alignedat}{-1}
&\del_t u-\Delta u+(u\cdot\nabla) u  +\nabla p   =  0,
 \\
&  \nabla \cdot u  = 0,
\end{alignedat}\right.  \tag{NS}$$

where $u: \mathbb R^3\times [0,T]\to\mathbb R^3$ denotes the velocity of the incompressible fluid, $p:\mathbb R^3\times [0,T]\to\mathbb R$ the pressure field. We are focused on the non-uniqueness of weak solutions to (1), where the weak solutions are defined as follows:

## 1.1 Previous works and our main results

In the pioneer paper (L), Leray proved that for any initial datum $u_0\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)$, there exists a global weak solutions to the equations (1) in $C_w([0, T]; L^2(\mathbb R^3)) \cap L^2([0, T]; \dot{H}^1(\mathbb R^3))$ with the energy inequality

$$\|u(t)\|_{L^2}^{2}+2\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla u(s)\|_{L^2}^{2}{\rm d s}\leq \|u_0\|_{L^2}^{2},\quad \forall \,t\in[0,T].$$

And this result was further developed by Hopf (Hopf) in smooth bounded domain, with Dirichlet boundary conditions. This class of weak solutions is now called as *Leray-Hopf weak solutions*. As discussed in (BV-19; Hopf; JS; Lady2), the uniqueness for Leray-Hopf weak solutions of the equations (1) remains an important open problem in the theory of the Navier-Stokes equations.

In order to have a clearer understanding of how far we are from solving this challenging problem, many researchers are dedicated to finding sufficient conditions that guarantee the uniqueness of Leray-Hopf weak solutions. The Serrin type criterions established by (ESS; KS; Lady; Prodi; Serr) shows that the Leray-Hopf weak solution is unique in $L^p_tL^q_x$ with $\frac{2}{p}+\frac{3}{q}\le 1$. In fact, Fabes et al. in (FJR) proved that this Serrin type condition except for $q=3$ also plays the role of a uniqueness criterion for *very weak solution* of the equations (1). The uniqueness in the endpoint case $C_tL^3_x$ for very weak solution was shown by Furioli et al. in (FLT).

In recent years, there have been major progresses in the non-uniqueness problems for weak solutions, and various works toward non-uniqueness of Leray-Hopf weak solutions. Jia and Šverák (JS14; JS) showed the non-uniqueness of Leray-Hopf weak solutions in $L^\infty_tL^{3,\infty}_x$ provided that a spectral condition holds. Guillod and Šverák (GS) give convincing numerical evidence of this spectral condition. Recently, Albritton, Brué and Colombo (ABC) proved the non-uniqueness of the Leray-Hopf weak solutions for the forced 3D Navier-Stokes equations by adapting properly Vishik’s construction into the cross section of an axisymmetric vortex ring. In addition to approaches based on spectral analysis, many studies have explored the non-uniqueness of weak solutions by methods involving convex integration. In the breakthrough work (BV), Buckmaster and Vicol obtained non-unique distributional solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations in $C_tL^2(\mathbb{T}^3)$. They developed a new convex integration scheme in Sobolev spaces using intermittent Beltrami flows which combined concentrations and oscillations. Furthermore, they jointly with Colombo (BCV) presented the first example of a mild/weak solution to the Navier-Stokes equation on torus whose singular set of times is nonempty, and has Hausdorff dimension strictly less than 1. Luo and Titi (LT) proved the non-uniqueness of weak solutions in $C_tL^2(\mathbb{T}^3)$ for the Navier–Stokes equations with fractional hyperviscosity $(-\Delta)^{\theta}$, whenever the exponent $(-\Delta)^{\theta}$ is less than $5/4$. For the stochastic 3D Navier-Stokes equations, Hofmanová, Zhu and Zhu (zhu1; zhu2; zhu3) established a series of works on the global existence and non-uniquenes. Remarkably, Cheskidov and Luo (1Cheskidov) proved the nonuniqueness of very weak solutions in the class $L^p_tL^q(\mathbb{T}^3)$ for $1\le p<2$ by exploiting the temporal intermittency in the convex integrations scheme, and this result implies the sharpness of the Ladyzhenskaya-Prodi-Serrin criteria $\frac{2}{p}+\frac{3}{q}\le 1$ at the endpoint $(p,q)=(2,\infty)$. The approach involving convex integration also has been applied to various other models. For instance, the Euler equations (Buc; BDIS15; BDS; DS17; DRS; DS09; DS14; zhu4; Ise17; Ise18; Ise22) and references therein, the stationary Navier-Stokes equations (Luo), the transport equations (BCD; CL21; CL22; MoS; MS), the MHD equations (2Beekie; LZZ; MY), and the Boussinesq equations (MNY; TZ17; TZ18).

The previous works (e.g. (BCV; BV; 1Cheskidov)) on the non-uniqueness of weak solutions for the Navier-Stokes equations within the convex integration scheme are established for the periodic case, and the iterative scheme in these works cannot be directly applied to the Cauchy problem in $\mathbb R^3$, etc.

In this paper, we aim to develop a new convex integration scheme to construct non-unique weak solutions of (1) with finite kinetic energy in $\mathbb R^3$:

By choosing $e(t)$ and $\widetilde{e}(t)$ such that $e(t)\neq \widetilde{e}(t)$ for $t> \tfrac{T}{2}$, Theorem 1.1 immediately shows that there exist infinitely many weak solutions in $C_tL^2(\mathbb R^3)$ for (1) with the same initial data. Particularly, weak solutions that dissipate the kinetic energy in $C_tL^2(\mathbb R^3)$ are not unique via choosing monotonically non-increasing functions $e(t)$ and $\widetilde{e}(t)$. ## 1.2 Main ideas

The proof of Theorem 1.1 draws upon several fundamental ideas introduced by the work (BV) of Buckmaster and Vicol, which was established in the periodic setting. In constructing nonperiodic solutions in $\mathbb R^3$, we cannot proceed with the iterative scheme as in (BV), since we have to confront the issue that the Reynolds stress may not maintain the property of spatial compactly support, which did not arise in the previous work in the periodic setting. However, due to the limitations of current geometric lemma, it seems necessary for the Reynolds error to be with compact support at each iteration step. This compels us to develop a new iterative scheme which enables us to control the support of the Reynolds stress within the context of the whole space $\mathbb R^3$.

To ensure that the Reynolds tensor has both compact support and divergence form at the next step, we cannot use the the inverse of the divergence operator due to the fact that a function with compact support, when acted upon by the inverse of the divergence operator, may not retain compact support in the whole space. Another difficulty comes from the fact that the absence of compact support in the approximate solution hinders the maintenance of the compact support property for the Reynolds tensor at the next step. In this paper, we develop a new iterative scheme to ensure the compatibility between the Reynolds stress error with compact support, divergence-form, and the non-compact support property of the approximate solution at each step.

For given $u^{\text{non-loc}}_q$ without compact support, the remaining part of $u_q$, we introduce a *localized corrector* $w^{\textup{(ns)}}_{q+1}$ such that $u^{\text{non-loc}}_{q+1}=u^{\text{non-loc}}_{\ell_q}+w^{\textup{(ns)}}_{q+1}$. As previously analyzed, without using the divergence inverse operator and the non-compact support property of the approximate solution give rise to some new tensor errors with non-divergence and non-compact support. Benefiting from the high frequency of flows, as shown in Lemma 1, one could expect that these errors are small. This observation inspires us to treat these errors as a forcing terms of a incompressible Navier-Stokes equations (see (3.2.2) below), and to define the localized corrector $w^{\textup{(ns)}}_{q+1}$ to be the solution of such equations. Subsequently, the localized corrector $w^{\textup{(ns)}}_{q+1}$ cancels these errors with non-divergence or non-compact support. This leads to the new Reynolds tensor error maintaining a compact support, allowing the iteration to proceed successfully.

To our knowledge, this is the first work of constructing a non-periodic weak solution to the Navier-Stokes equations through convex integration method. The new iterative scheme developed in this paper can be also applied for other related issues to the Navier-Stokes equations or other viscous models.

## 1.3 Applications to other problems

As a matter of fact, the main idea of developing a new iterative scheme via refining approximation solutions is applicable not only to the whole space, but also to general domains. For instance, we present the non-uniqueness result of weak solutions for the Navier-Stokes equations in smooth bounded domain. Furthermore, we also present a result of instability near the Couette flow.

We are in position to state our two applications.

### 1.3.1 Application : The non-uniqueness result in smooth bounded domain 

We consider the incompressible Navier-Stokes equation in smooth bounded domain $\mathcal{D}$:

$$\left\{ \begin{alignedat}{-1}
&\del_t v-\Delta v+(v\cdot\nabla) v  +\nabla p   =  0,\quad{\rm in}\quad {\mathcal{D}}\times(0,T],
 \\
&  \nabla \cdot v  = 0, \quad\qquad\qquad \qquad \qquad\,\,\,\, \, {\rm in}\quad  {\mathcal{D}}\times(0,T],\\
& v=0,  \quad\qquad\qquad \qquad \qquad \quad \, \, \,\, \,  \, \, \, \,  {\rm on}\quad  {\partial\mathcal{D}}\times[0,T].
\end{alignedat}\right. \tag{1}$$

Here a vector field $v\in C([0,T];L^2(\mathcal{D}))$ is called a weak solution to (1) if it solves (1) in the sense of distribution. It seems to be the first result on constructing non-unique weak solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations in a bounded non-periodic domain via the convex integration method. The proof is provided in Section 5. The readers will see that the iterative scheme used in the proof differs slightly from the previous one in the proof of Theorem 1.1, and thereby this iterative scheme has a certain degree of flexibility and allows us to address different issues.

### 1.3.2 Application : The instability of the system (1) near Couette flow 

Let $U=(x_2,0,0)\in\mathbb R^3$ be the 3D Couette flow. Employing the iterative scheme in this paper enables us to obtain the following instability result for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations (1) near the Couette flow in $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$.

Hydrodynamic stability at high Reynolds number has been a very active ﬁeld in the ﬂuid mechanics. There is a series of work on the stability threshold problem, e.g. (BGM17; BGM20; BGM22; CWZ; DM23; WZ) for the 3D Couette ﬂow. As a simple application of the convex integration method, we present an instability result for the (1), which corresponds to the ill-posedness of the perturbation system near the 3D Couette ﬂow in $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$.

# 2 Induction scheme

In this section, we give the induction scheme and the two iterative propositions, that is Proposition 2.2 and Proposition 2.2 below, which enable us to prove Theorem 1.1.

## 2.1 Parameters

First of all, we introduce several parameters. Let

$$\begin{align*}

b=2^{15}, \quad\beta=b^{-4},  \quad 0<\alpha\leq b^{-7}. \tag{2}\end{align*}$$

Suppose that $a\in \mathbb N$ is a large number depending on $b,\beta,\alpha$ and the initial data $u^{\textup{in}}$. We define

$$\begin{align*}

    \lambda_q :=   a^{b^q},  \quad \delta_q :=  \lambda_q^{-2\beta}, \quad \ell_q:=\lambda^{-60}_q,\quad q\ge 0, \tag{3}\end{align*}$$

and

$$\begin{align*}

\Omega_{q}:=\big[-\tfrac{1}{2} +\lambda_q^{-\alpha},~
\tfrac{1}{2} -\lambda_q^{-\alpha}  \big]^3   ,~~~~q\geq1. \tag{4}\end{align*}$$

For given $e(t)$ and $\widetilde{e}(t)$ in Theorem 1.1, there exists an appropriate small constant $c$ such that $c\delta_2<e(t),\widetilde{e}(t)<\frac{3}{c}\delta_2$ for $t\in [0, T]$. Without loss of generality, we set $c=1$.

## 2.2 Iterative procedure 

As is usual in convex integration schemes, we consider the following relaxation of the Navier-Stokes equations

$$\tag{NSR}
\left\{ \begin{alignedat}{-1}
   & \del_t u_q-\Delta u_q+\text{div}(u_q\otimes u_q) +\nabla p_q   =\text{div}\mathring R_q,
 \\
  &\nabla \cdot u_q = 0, \\
\end{alignedat}\right.$$

where the *Reynolds stress* $\mathring R_q$ is a symmetric trace-free $3\times3$ matrix.

To employ induction, we suppose that the solution $(u_q, p_q, \mathring R_q)$ of the equations (2.2) on $(0, T]\times \mathbb R^3$ satisfies the following conditions:

$$\begin{align*}
&u_q=u^{\text{loc}}_q+u^{\text{non-loc}}_q, \tag{5}\\
&\|u^{\text{loc}}_q\|_{L^{\infty}_tL^2}\leq\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}C_0\delta^{1/2}_{j+1},\qquad\|u^{\text{non-loc}}_q\|_{\widetilde L^{\infty}_tB^{1/2}_{2,1} } \le \sum_{j=0}^{q-1}\lambda^{-1}_{j}, \tag{6}\\
&\|(u^{\text{loc}}_q,~u^{\text{non-loc}}_q)\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}H^5} \leq \lambda^{10}_q, \tag{7}\\
    &\| \mathring R_q \|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^1 }  \le \delta_{q+1}\lambda_q^{-4 \alpha}, \qquad\| \mathring R_q \|_{L^{\infty}_{t}W^{5,1} }  \le  \lambda_q^{10}, \tag{8}\\
     &{\text{spt}_{x}} u^{\text{loc}}_q, {\text{spt}_{x}} \mathring R_q\subseteq \Omega_q   , \tag{9}\\
    &\delta_{q+1}\leq e(t)-\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}|u_q|^2\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x \leq 3\delta_{q+1}, \quad 0\le t\le T. \tag{10}\end{align*}$$

Here $C_0$ is a universal large enough number. The following proposition shows that there exists a solution $(u_{q+1}, p_{q+1}, \mathring R_{q+1})$ of the equations (2.2) satisfying the above inductive conditions (5)–(10) with $q$ replaced by $q+1$, which guarantees the iteration proceeds successfully.

## 2.3 Proof of Theorem 1.1

For given $e(t)$ and $\widetilde{e}(t)$, let $(u_1, p_1, \mathring R_1)=(0,0,0)$. One easily verifies that $(u_1, p_1, \mathring R_1)$ satisfies (2.2) and (5)–(10), as well as (10) with $e(t)$ replaced by $\widetilde{e}(t)$. Utilizing Proposition 2.2 inductively, we obtain a sequence of solutions $\{(u_q, p_q,\mathring R_q)\}$ and $\{(\widetilde{u}_q, \widetilde{p}_q, \widetilde{\mathring R}_q)\}$ of the equations (2.2) respectively satisfying estimates (5)–(2.2), and (5)–(2.2) with $e(t)$ replaced by $\widetilde{e}(t)$. By the definition of $\delta_q$, one can easily deduce that $\sum_{i=2}^{\infty}\delta^{1/2}_{i}$ converges to a finite number. This fact combined with (2.2) implies that $\{u_q\}$ and $\{\widetilde{u}_q\}$ are two Cauchy sequences in $C_tL^2( \mathbb R^3)$. Since $\|(\mathring R_q, {\mathring {\widetilde{R}}}_q)\|_{L^\infty_t L^1}\rightarrow 0$ as $q\to\infty$, the limit functions $u$ and $\widetilde{u}$ are weak solutions of the Navier-Stokes equation (1) and satisfies

$$\begin{align*}
    &\int_{\mathbb R^3}| u(t,\cdot)|^2\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x=e(t),~~~~t\in[0,T], \tag{11}\\
    &\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\widetilde{u}(t,\cdot)|^2\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x=\widetilde{e}(t),~~~~t\in[0,T]. \tag{12}\end{align*}$$
Since $e(t)=\widetilde{e}(t)$ for $t\in[0, \tfrac{T}{2}]$, Proposition 2.2 implies that $u(0,x)=\widetilde{u}(0,x)$. This relation combined with (11) and (12) shows Theorem 1.1.

# 3 Proof of Proposition 2.2

In this section, we are devoted to the proof of Proposition 2.2. More specifically, we construct $(u_{q+1}, p_{q+1}, \mathring R_{q+1})$ in Proposition 2.2 by the following two steps:

1.  Step 1: Mollification: $(u_q, p_q, \mathring R_q)\mapsto (u_{\ell_q},  p_{\ell_q}, \mathring R_{\ell_q})$. We define $(u_{\ell_q},  p_{\ell_q}, \mathring R_{\ell_q})$ by mollifying $(u_q, p_q, \mathring R_q)$ so that we obtain higher regularity estimates for the perturbation.

2.  Step 2: Perturbation: $(u_{\ell_q},  p_{\ell_q}, \mathring R_{\ell_q})\mapsto (u_{q+1}, p_{q+1}, \mathring R_{q+1})$. By making use of the box flows introduced in (MY), the temporal corrector inspired by (BV) and the localized corrector , we construct the perturbation $w_{q+1}$. Then we define $u_{q+1}$ by adding $w_{q+1}$ on $u_{\ell_q}$.

## 3.1 Mollification

We define the functions $(u_{\ell_q},  p_{\ell_q}, \mathring R_{\ell_q})$ by the spatial mollifier $\psi_{\ell_q}$ and the time mollifier $\varphi_{\ell_q}$ in Definition 1 as follows: For $(x,t)\in \mathbb R^3\times [0, T-\ell_q]$,

$$\begin{align*}
   & u_{\ell_q} (x,t):=\int_t^{t+\ell_q}(u_q* \psi_{\ell_q})(x,s)\varphi_{\ell_q}(t-s)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s, \tag{13}\\
   &u^{\text{loc}}_{\ell_q}(x,t):=\int_t^{t+\ell_q}(u^{\text{loc}}_q* \psi_{\ell_q})(x,s)\varphi_{\ell_q}(t-s)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s, \tag{14}\\
      &u^{\text{non-loc}}_{\ell_q}(x,t):=\int_t^{t+\ell_q}(u^{\text{non-loc}}_q* \psi_{\ell_q})(x,s)\varphi_{\ell_q}(t-s)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s, \tag{15}\\
   &p_{\ell_q}(x,t):=\int_t^{t+\ell_q}(p_q * \psi_{\ell_q})(x,s)\varphi_{\ell_q}(t-s)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s, \tag{16}\\
 &   \mathring R_{\ell_q}(x,t) := \int_t^{t+\ell_q}(\mathring R_q * \psi_{\ell_q})(x,s)\varphi_{\ell_q}(t-s)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s, \tag{17}\\
 &R^{\text{rem}}_q:=  u_{\ell_q} \otimes u_{\ell_q} - \int_t^{t+\ell_q}((u_q \otimes u_q) * \psi_{\ell_q})(x,s)\varphi_{\ell_q}(t-s)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s. \tag{18}\end{align*}$$

One easily verifies that $(u_{\ell_q},  p_{\ell_q}, \mathring R_{\ell_q}, R^{\text{rem}}_q)$ solves the Cauchy problem

$$\left\{ \begin{alignedat}{-1}
&\del_t u_{\ell_q}-\Delta u_{\ell_q}+\text{div}(u_{\ell_q}\otimes u_{\ell_q})  +\nabla p_{\ell_q}   =  \text{div}\mathring R_{\ell_q} +\text{div}R^{\text{rem}}_q,
\\
 & \nabla \cdot u_{\ell_q} = 0,
  \\
  &  u_{\ell_q} |_{t=0}=   \int_0^{\ell_q}(u_q * \psi_{\ell_q})(x,s)\varphi_{\ell_q}(-s)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s
\end{alignedat}\right. \tag{19}$$

such that

$$\begin{align*}
&\text{spt}_x u^{\text{loc}}_{\ell_q}, \,\text{spt}_x \mathring R_{\ell_q} \subseteq \Omega_{q}+[-\lambda^{-1}_q, \lambda^{-1}_q]^3. \tag{20}\end{align*}$$

Moreover, $(u_{\ell_q}, \mathring R_{\ell_q}, R^{\text{rem}}_q)$ satisfies the following estimates.

## 3.2 Perturbation

The principle perturbation is mainly composed of two parts: amplitudes and the intermittent building blocks.  
*Amplitudes*We define amplitudes firstly. Let $\chi:[0,\infty)\to [1,\infty)$ be a smooth function satisfying

$$\chi(z)=\left\{ \begin{alignedat}{-1}
&1, \quad 0\le z\le 1,\\
&z, \quad z\ge 2,
\end{alignedat}\right. \tag{21}$$

with $z\le 2\chi(z)\le 4z$ for $z\in (1,2)$. We define that

$$\chi_q:=\chi\Big(\Big\langle\tfrac{\mathring R_{\ell_q}}{\delta_{q+1}\lambda^{-2\alpha}_q}\Big\rangle\Big)
,\quad \text{where}\,\,\big\langle\cdot \big\rangle:=\sqrt{1+|\cdot|^2}.$$

Next, the space cutoffs $\{\eta_q(x)\}_{q\ge 1}\in C^{\infty}_c(\mathbb R^3)$ are defined by

$$\text{spt}\,\,\eta_{q}=\Omega_{q+1} , \quad\quad   \eta_q|_{\Omega_{q}+ [ -\lambda^{-1}_q ,\lambda^{-1}_q ]^3}\equiv 1,\quad~~\quad|D^N\eta_q|\lesssim \lambda^{N}_q\,\,\text{for}\,\,N\ge 0, \tag{22}$$

where $\Omega_{q+1}$ is defined in (4). Thanks to (20), one can easily deduce that

$$\begin{align*}

\eta_{q}\mathring R_{\ell_{q}}=\mathring R_{ \ell_{q}}. \tag{23}\end{align*}$$

We claim that

$$\begin{align*}

  \frac{1}{2}\le \int_{\mathbb R^3}\eta^2_q\chi_q\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x
   \le 5. \tag{24}\end{align*}$$

Indeed, we deduce from the definitions of $\eta_q$ and $\chi_q$ that

$$\begin{align*}
  \int_{\mathbb R^3}\eta^2_q\chi_q\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x=\int_{\Omega_{q+1}}\eta_q^2(x)\chi\Big(\Big\langle\tfrac{\mathring R_{\ell_q}}{\delta_{q+1}\lambda^{-2\alpha}_q}\Big\rangle\Big)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x.
\end{align*}$$

On one hand, from (3.1), one has

$$\begin{align*}
   \int_{\Omega_{q+1}}\eta_q^2(x)\chi\Big(\Big\langle\tfrac{\mathring R_{\ell_q}}{\delta_{q+1}\lambda^{-2\alpha}_q}\Big\rangle\Big)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x
   \le&\int_{\Omega_{q+1}}4\big(1+\big|\tfrac{\mathring R_{\ell_q}}{\delta_{q+1}\lambda^{-2\alpha}_q}\big|\big)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\le 5. \tag{25}\end{align*}$$

On the other hand,

$$\begin{align*}
   &\int_{\Omega_{q+1}}\eta_q^2(x)\chi\Big(\Big\langle\tfrac{\mathring R_{\ell_q}}{\delta_{q+1}\lambda^{-4\alpha}_q}\Big\rangle\Big)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x
   \ge\int_{\Omega_{q}}1\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\ge\frac{1}{2}.
\end{align*}$$

We define

$$\begin{align*}

\rho_q(t) =   \frac{1}{3\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\eta^2_q\chi_{q}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x}\Big(e(t) - \int_{\mathbb R^3}  |u_{\ell_q}|^2 \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x - 2{\delta_{q+2}} \Big). \tag{26}\end{align*}$$

Then (3.1) and (24) together show that

$$\begin{align*}

   \frac{1}{60}\delta_{q+1}\le\rho_q(t)\le 3\delta_{q+1} \tag{27}\end{align*}$$

Moreover, by (3.1), (3.1) and the definition of $\rho_q(t)$ in (26), we see

$$\begin{align*}
\|\partial_t\rho_q(t)\|_{L^\infty_{t,x}}\lesssim &\delta_{q+1}\|\partial_t\chi_q\|_{L^\infty_{t,x}}+\|u_{\ell_q}\|_{L^\infty_t L^2}\|\partial_t u_{\ell_q}\|_{L^\infty_t L^2}\\
\lesssim &\lambda^{20}_{q}\ell^{-1}_q. \tag{28}\end{align*}$$

We are in position to give the amplitudes $a_{(k,q)}(t,x)$ by

$$a_{(k,q)}(t,x)=\eta_{q}
 a_k\Big({\rm Id}-\frac{\mathring R_{\ell_{q}}}{\chi_{q}\rho_q}\Big)
 (\chi_q \rho_q)^{1/2}, \tag{29}$$

### 3.2.1 Estimates for amplitudes $a_{(k,q)}$

### 3.2.2 Construction the perturbation

  
*Building blocks*Assume that $\Phi:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is a smooth cutoff function supported on the interval $(0, \lambda^{-1}_1]$ and $\int_{\mathbb R} \Phi''(x) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x=0$. We set $\phi=\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x^2}\Phi$ and normalize it in such a way that

$$\begin{align*}

\int_{\mathbb{R}}\phi^2\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x=1. \tag{35}\end{align*}$$

For any small positive parameter $r$ such that $r^{-1}\in\mathbb Z$, we define

$$\begin{align*}

\phi_{r}(x) :=r^{-\frac{1}{2}}\phi (r^{-1}x),\qquad \Phi_{r}(x) :=r^{-\frac{1}{2}}\Phi (r^{-1}x). \tag{36}\end{align*}$$

We periodize $\phi_r$ and $\Phi_r$ so that the resulting functions are periodic functions defined on $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}=:\mathbb{T}$, and we still denote the $\mathbb{T}$-periodic functions by $\phi_r$ and $\Phi_r$. Next, we choose a large number $N_{\Lambda}$ such that $N_{\Lambda}{k}\in \mathbb{Z}^3$ for all $k\in\Lambda$, where $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{S}^2\cap\mathbb{Q}^3$ is denoted in Remark A.

Let $r=\lambda^{-3/4}_{q+1}$ and $\mu=\lambda^{5/4}_{q+1}$, we define

$$\begin{align*}
&\phi_{k,r}(x): =\phi_{r}( N_{\Lambda}k\cdot x),\,\,\phi_{\bar{k},r, \mu}(x,t):=\phi_{r}( N_{\Lambda}(\bar{k}\cdot x+\mu t)),\,\,\phi_{\bar{\bar{k}},r}(x):=\phi_{r}( N_{\Lambda}\bar{\bar{k}}\cdot  x).
\end{align*}$$

Let $\sigma=\lambda^{1/16}_{q+1}$, we define

$$\begin{align*}
 &\phi_{k,r,\sigma}(x):= \phi_{k,r}(\sigma x)=N^{-1}_{\Lambda}r^{2}\sigma^{-1}\text{div}{\big((\Phi_{r})'( N_{\Lambda}k\cdot \sigma x)k\big)},
\end{align*}$$

where

$$\begin{align*}
\Phi’_{r}( N_{\Lambda}k\cdot \sigma x):=r(\Phi_{r})'(N_{\Lambda}k\cdot \sigma x).
\end{align*}$$

Therefore, we have

$$\begin{align*}
 &\phi_{k,r,\sigma}(x)=N^{-1}_{\Lambda}r\sigma^{-1}\text{div}{\big(\Phi'_{r}(N_{\Lambda}k\cdot \sigma x)k\big)}.
\end{align*}$$

Let

$$\begin{align*}
 &\phi_{\bar{k},r,\sigma, \mu}(x,t):=\phi_{\bar{k},r, \mu}(\sigma x,\sigma t)={N^{-1}_{\Lambda}r\sigma^{-1}}\text{div}{\big(\Phi'_{r}(\sigma N_{\Lambda}(\bar{k}\cdot x+\mu t))\bar{k}}\big),\\
 &\phi_{\bar{\bar{k}},r,\sigma}(x):=\phi_{\bar{\bar{k}},r}(\sigma x)=N^{-1}_{\Lambda}r\sigma^{-1}\text{div}{\big(\Phi'_{r}( N_{\Lambda}\bar{\bar{k}}\cdot \sigma x)\bar{\bar{k}}\big)}.
\end{align*}$$

Finally, we define a set of functions $\{\phi_{k,\bar{k},\bar{\bar{k}}}\}_{k\in\Lambda}$ and $\{\phi_{k,\bar{k},\bar{\bar{k}},\sigma}\}_{k\in\Lambda}:\mathbb{T}^3\times \mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ by

$$\begin{align*}
    \phi_{k,\bar{k},\bar{\bar{k}}}(x,t)=\phi_{k,r}(x)\phi_{\bar{k},r, \mu}(x,t)\phi_{\bar{\bar{k}},r}(x)
\end{align*}$$

and

$$\begin{align*}
\phi_{k,\bar{k},\bar{\bar{k}},\sigma}(x,t)
&:=\phi_{k,r,\sigma}(x-x_k)\phi_{\bar{k},r,\sigma, \mu}(x-x_k,t)\phi_{\bar{\bar{k}},r,\sigma}(x-x_k),\\
&= \phi_{k,\bar{k},\bar{\bar{k}}}(\sigma(x-x_k),\sigma t)
\end{align*}$$

where $\{x_k\}_{k\in\Lambda}$ are shifts which guarantee that

$$\begin{align*}

\phi_{k,\bar{k},\bar{\bar{k}},\sigma}\cdot\phi_{k',\bar{k}',\bar{\bar{k}}',\sigma}=0,
~~~k\neq k',~~k,k'\in\Lambda. \tag{37}\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}

From the definitions of $\phi_{k,\bar{k},\bar{\bar{k}}}$ and $\phi_{k,\bar{k},\bar{\bar{k}},\sigma}$, one easily concludes by $k\perp \bar{k}\perp \bar{\bar{k}}$ that

Before constructing the perturbation, we introduce $\psi,\Psi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T})$ such that $\psi=\Psi''$ and $\int_{\mathbb{T}}\Psi'\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x=0$. Then we define
